blocks.text: Michaelis in Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1080, on the authority of the Alexandrian and the Vulgate translator, interprets ילק as bruchus. He says that the bruchus is a little worm that creeps under the earth and lays waste roots with its bite (Engerling in German), which afterwards becomes winged and is called by us, from the month of May, Maykäfer. But to Jerome, Augustine and Remigius of Auxerre the bruchus is the young of the locust, as is clear from what Bochart cites below, p. 447 (in the marginal note). The Greek βροῦκος [broukos] or βρῦχος [brychos], moreover, signifies now the young of the locust, now a certain species of locust. And at Ierem. LI, 27 the Alexandrian translators expressly put for ילק ἀκρίδα [akrida], the best-known name of the locust. The Chaldee and the Syriac also understood a locust: the former renders פרחא, winged locust, the latter ܣܡܐܢ ܠܐ ܦܪܚ, locust not yet winged. So far, then, is Bochart from assuming at his pleasure that ילק is a locust, as Michaelis asserts, that it is rather Michaelis himself who deserves reproach, for departing without reason from the authority of the ancients. Michaelis is refuted at length by Oedmann, fasc. 2, ch. 6, p. 126 ff., who himself takes ילק for the gryllus cristatus Linn. (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 4, p. 2074), common in those lands. He is moved chiefly by Ierem. LI, 27, where ילק is called סמר, which Oedmann interprets as serrated and refers to the four-cleft keel of the thorax. But Tychsen, p. 91, renders the same סמר as bristling, which he judges to be an epithet of the gryllus haematopus Linn. (p. 2075), with its hairy-fringed thighs. Bochart will say more on ילק סמר below, Chapter 2.

In the Talmudic tractate חלין Cholir, the סלעם is said to have a bald head, and the female to lack the sword-shaped tail. Since Tychsen finds these marks in the species of locust that Asso places third (and p. 5–6 of the German trans.) and calls gryllus eversor, he is persuaded, p. 69, that the Hebrew סלעם is that same species.

To Michaelis in Supplemm. p. 2094, צלצל is the same as חסיל, the gryllus with mole's feet, the gryllus talpiformis, which he thinks was named from its shrill and sharp sound, following the authority of the Syriac translator, who puts ܨܪܨܘܪ, cricket. Against this opinion, however, not a few objections have been raised by Tychsen, p. 79–80, and Oedmann, fasc. 2, p. 140 ff., although the latter gave no opinion of his own on צלצל. To Tychsen it seems an onomatopoeic name of the gryllus stridulus Linn. (vol. 1, part 4, p. 2078). The Alexandrians render ἐρισυβην [erisybēn], which the Vulgate translator rendered rubigo [blight]. The same view pleased Jac. Hase in Biblioth. Brem. class 6, fasc. 5, diss. 1, § 9, who derives our word from צלה, he scorched, he burnt.

هذه الاسما كلها قد تكون الاصناف من الجراد [hādhihi al-asmā kulluhā qad takūn al-aṣnāf min al-jarād] all these names signify certain species of locusts, says R. Tanchum in his Commentary on Joel 1:4, cited by Edw. Pococke on the same place, p. 7.

Hence at the same time appears the emptiness of the opinion both of Andr. Norrelius (formerly librarian to the King of the Swedes), who in his Diatriba de avibus esu licitis Levit. XI, 22., Uppsala 1746, contradicting all the ancients and following no usage of the oriental languages, makes ארבה doves, סלעם geese, חרגל the gallinaceous kind, and חגב sparrows, [III, 260] understanding the four on which they go of the four toes of the feet; and also of J. D. Michaelis, who in his Questions proposed to those travelling to Arabia, p. 84 ff., and in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr., where he treats the individual names, thinks that what is designated is not certain species of locusts but four stages of their life, not considering that locusts cannot be eaten before they have begun to fly—to say nothing of the other objections raised against this opinion by Tychsen, p. 62 ff., and Oedmann, fasc. 2, p. 88 ff., who also refuted Norrelius's dreams more fully than was necessary.
Perhaps the Gryllus viridis of Forsskål (Descript. Animall. p. 81), with depressed, fringed thorax, spiny forelegs, and a yellow spot on each elytron. Common in the gardens of Alexandria.

To these add, from Niebuhr's Descript. Arab. p. 171, the red locust, Dsjerâd áchmar [جراد احمر] [jarād aḥmar], a migratory one, which when it first arrives in the regions of Arabia is small and lean, but after it has grown up, to the great damage of the crops, is called Dsjerâd Mükken [جران مكن [jarān mkn] i.e. a locust full of eggs], and is counted among delicacies by the Arabs.

Among the people of Basra جراد عصغور [jarād ʿṣghūr] is the male of the Mukn مكن [mkn], the fertile egg-bearer, as Niebuhr attests, p. 171. I shall add his own words: At Basra the locust which the Arabs most like to eat was called Mukn. It was further added that this is the female, and very fat, or full of eggs, and that it is a strengthening food for men. Dsjerad asfur is the male of the Mukn, but lean, and is therefore not much used for eating at Basra.
